title: Voyager 1 Goes Silent on Its Milestone Day — Data Stops as Probe Crosses One Light-Day

content:
NASA’s Voyager 1 crossed one light-day from Earth on Wednesday — the farthest any human-made object has ever traveled — and did it in silence. The spacecraft stopped sending science and engineering data on Nov. 14, NASA said, and engineers still do not know why.

A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, locked onto the spacecraft and received its carrier signal — the radio wave that carries data — but no data came with it. The carrier signal means Voyager 1’s attitude control computer is still keeping its antenna pointed at Earth and its broadcast equipment still works, NASA said. The problem appears to be with the onboard computer that gathers data from the spacecraft’s subsystems and formats it for transmission.

The milestone still stands. Voyager 1 reached one light-day — about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) — at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern on Nov. 18, and NASA planned to formally confirm it today, Nov. 19, using the carrier signal and trajectory calculations. The probe travels at a consistent speed on a known trajectory and has no way to change its speed, NASA noted, so the engineering problem cannot change when it crossed the line.

Diagnosing the problem will be slow. A radio signal takes 24 hours to reach the probe, and any reply takes another 24 hours to come back — so even a simple test spans two days, and NASA said finding the cause may take weeks or longer.

Engineers are also checking whether the outage is connected to a brief communications gap in October, when the mission lost all contact with the spacecraft for about 48 hours. Voyager 1 resumed communication on its own and operated normally until Nov. 14.

This is not the first time the probe has gone quiet this way. In 2023, ground controllers received a carrier signal but no data from Voyager 1, an issue traced to one of its onboard computers. NASA said the team’s experience resolving that problem is informing its approach now.

Voyager 1 launched Sept. 5, 1977, and has been the most distant human-made object since passing Pioneer 10 in 1998. It entered interstellar space in August 2012. Its twin, Voyager 2, is 13.5 billion miles out and will not reach one light-day until November 2035.

NASA and the mission planned to celebrate the light-day milestone today, Nov. 19 — a day after it was reached — with a live event at noon Eastern from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The mission turns 50 in 2027. NASA said it expects to eventually lose both spacecraft to unresolvable engineering issues, but plans to do everything it can to keep them operating and delivering science for as long as possible. As of this writing, NASA has not announced that data return has been restored.

Sources: NASA Science, Nov. 18, 2026; Popular Science, Nov. 18, 2026.
